title: Astrid and the Debt
premise: Mirabel Okafor, a whistle-blower living under four names—including his current identity as 'Astrid Lindqvist'—witnesses the impossible: a passenger flight erased from every radar, database, and memory mid-flight. Aboard that plane was his only contact inside a defense contractor, carrying proof of a sold-out witness-protection pipeline. Hunted by an assassin who seems to know each of his four names before he uses them, Mirabel must smuggle the truth through three governments' bureaucracies of complicity. In the end, he survives not by running but by surrendering his final name—publishing everything as 'Astrid,' a person who never existed—and letting Mirabel Okafor die on paper at last.
about_author: Freya Lockridge is a former aviation-industry analyst who left the sector after a records dispute she still won't discuss. She writes thrillers from a coastal town in Norway, where she keeps, she admits, a go-bag out of habit.

chapters.title: Four Names, One Bag
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. We meet 'Astrid Lindqvist' in Oslo: meticulous routines, a packed go-bag, a polished cover story as a freelance translator. A coded message from his insider contact, 'Vesper,' promises explosive documents on flight KL-407. The beat is controlled paranoia—the calm before erasure.

chapters.title: The Flight That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Vesper boards KL-407 to hand off the drive; mid-flight, the aircraft vanishes from trackers, booking systems, and news feeds—as if it never existed. Mirabel finds Vesper's dead-drop empty except for a single burned corner of paper. Emotional beat: vertigo, the ground dissolving under a man built on paperwork.

chapters.title: The Man Who Knows Your Mother's Name
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, with a chilling interlude from the assassin, 'Cutter,' who recites all four of Mirabel's names like a shopping list. First assassination attempt disguised as a burglary. Beat: the hunter isn't guessing—he's reading a script Mirabel thought was private.

chapters.title: Go-Bag Protocol
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He burns his Oslo life and runs to Rotterdam under name three, 'Daniel Reyes.' He reconstructs Vesper's research: a witness-protection pipeline selling protected people to the very corporations they exposed—and KL-407 was its cleanup crew. Beat: grief sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Embassy Queue
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. He approaches a Dutch intelligence officer, Ilse Brandt, offering testimony; her superiors stall him with forms and smiles while quietly flagging his location. Brandt's own POV reveals her doubt—she's seen 'erased' cases before. Beat: hope curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: Safe House, Unsafe Hands
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Brandt and Cutter. The safe house is compromised from inside; Cutter arrives not to kill but to recruit, offering Mirabel his old life back if he surrenders the drive. Mirabel escapes through a canal lock, wounded. Beat: betrayal made physical.

chapters.title: What Vesper Left Behind
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Following Vesper's obsession with redundancy, he finds the full archive hidden in a decommissioned lighthouse archive—proof naming officials in three governments. He also learns Vesper boarded KL-407 voluntarily, trading himself to buy Mirabel time. Beat: devastating inheritance.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Deadline
chapters.summary: Mirabel and a now-convinced Brandt race to leak simultaneously to press outlets in three countries before a coordinated summit buries the scandal. Cutter closes in, and Brandt is taken. Beat: rising dread, the clock audible in every sentence.

chapters.title: Astrid
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, climax. At a Baltic ferry terminal he confronts Cutter—not with violence but with broadcast: the archive uploads live as they speak, mirrored beyond anyone's reach. Cutter's employers disown him in real time. Beat: the assassin's certainty shattering against a truth already loose.

chapters.title: The Name He Buried
chapters.summary: Mirabel's/Brandt's shared epilogue-POV. The scandal breaks; hearings begin; some guilty men fall, others merely shuffle. Mirabel formally declares 'Mirabel Okafor' dead and publishes his memoir under 'Astrid' alone. Final beat: bittersweet freedom—an identity chosen, finally, instead of imposed.
